title: Handling conflict: the Thomas-Kilmann modes
blurb: Place the five Thomas-Kilmann modes on the assertiveness and cooperativeness axes, and choose the right one for each conflict situation.
question: On a station upgrade, a contractor is about to work beside a live rail line without a safety permit, two design leads disagree about a key interface with weeks to resolve it, and two clerks are squabbling over a meeting room. Should the project manager handle all three conflicts the same way? Which Thomas-Kilmann mode suits each?

teach.body: The Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (TKI) describes behaviour in conflict on two dimensions. Assertiveness is how far you try to satisfy your own concerns; cooperativeness is how far you try to satisfy the other party's. Combining them gives five modes: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating. In plain English: how hard do I push for what I want, and how much do I help them get what they want? No mode is best: each suits different situations.

teach.h: The five modes on two axes
teach.caption: Vertical axis: assertiveness (satisfying my own concerns). Competing and accommodating are opposites, as are collaborating and avoiding.

teach.h: Collaborating vs compromising: the classic mix-up
How a project manager uses TKI
teach.body: First diagnose the situation: How important is the issue? How important is the relationship? How much time is there? What is the balance of power? Is safety or the law at stake? Then choose the mode that fits, rather than always using your favourite. Most people have a natural default mode; knowing yours helps you notice when it is the wrong tool. Over a project, a good project manager uses all five.

rows.label: Time pressure
values: Fixed time box: compromise on scope

teach.caption: Iterative cultures lean towards collaboration, but a fixed time box often means compromising on which items make it in.

teach.text: Two classic traps. 1. AVOIDING is low assertive AND low cooperative (sidestep or postpone). ACCOMMODATING is low assertive but HIGH cooperative (give way to them). 2. COMPROMISING is NOT win-win: each side gives something up. Only COLLABORATING aims for both sides to be fully satisfied.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the model and its two dimensions: assertiveness and cooperativeness.
Name the mode that fits the scenario and place it on the two axes.
Explain why it fits: urgency, importance, relationship, time or power.
Note a limitation or risk of that mode (e.g. competing breeds resentment).
State that no mode is always best: the project manager adapts to the situation.
TKI axes: assertiveness (own concerns) and cooperativeness (others' concerns).
Competing: high/low; emergencies and quick decisions.
Collaborating: high/high; win-win on important issues when time allows.
Compromising: medium/medium; split the difference, expedient or temporary fixes.
Avoiding: low/low, for trivial issues or cooling off. Accommodating: low/high, to preserve relationships or when wrong.

summary: You can now describe the Thomas-Kilmann model's two dimensions and place all five conflict modes on them. You can also choose the mode that suits a given project situation and explain the risk of relying on any one mode too much.

A.q: Which Thomas-Kilmann mode combines high assertiveness with low cooperativeness?
A.why: Competing means pursuing your own concerns at the other party's expense: high assertive, low cooperative.

whyNot.0: Collaborating is high on both dimensions.
whyNot.1: Accommodating is the opposite: low assertive, high cooperative.
whyNot.2: Compromising is moderate on both dimensions.

A.q: Which mode aims for a win-win outcome by fully satisfying the concerns of both parties?
A.why: Collaborating is high in both assertiveness and cooperativeness, working through the issue to find a solution that fully meets both sides' concerns.

whyNot.0: Compromising means each side gives something up, so neither is fully satisfied.
whyNot.2: Accommodating satisfies the other party at the expense of your own concerns.

A.q: What are the two dimensions used in the Thomas-Kilmann model?
options: Power and interest in the project
Probability and impact of a risk
Urgency and importance of the task
A.why: TKI plots conflict behaviour on assertiveness (satisfying your own concerns) and cooperativeness (satisfying the other party's concerns).

whyNot.1: Power and interest are the axes of the stakeholder grid.
whyNot.2: Probability and impact are used to assess risk.
whyNot.3: Urgency and importance belong to time-management prioritisation, not TKI.

B.q: A site supervisor sees a subcontractor about to enter an excavation that has not been made safe. Which conflict mode is most appropriate?
B.why: An immediate safety risk needs a quick, firm decision: competing (stop the work now) is appropriate in emergencies.

whyNot.0: Collaborating takes time that a safety emergency does not allow.
whyNot.1: Safety cannot be half-met by splitting the difference.
whyNot.3: Avoiding would leave a person in danger.

B.q: Two team members are arguing heatedly over a minor formatting choice in a report, and tempers are high. What does the Thomas-Kilmann model suggest?
B.why: For trivial issues, or when people need time to cool off, avoiding (sidestepping or postponing) is appropriate.

whyNot.1: Imposing a decision on a trivial issue may inflame tempers further.
whyNot.2: Collaborating takes time and effort the issue doesn't merit.
whyNot.3: Compromising is possible, but the issue is too trivial and emotions too high to negotiate now.

B.q: A project manager realises, during a dispute with the lead engineer, that the engineer's method is actually better. Which mode is most appropriate?
B.why: Accommodating (giving way) suits situations where you are wrong, or the relationship matters more than the point.

whyNot.0: Pushing a method you now know is worse would harm the project.
whyNot.1: There is no need to work up a joint solution: the engineer's method is simply better.
whyNot.2: There is nothing to split: the engineer's method is simply better.

C.q: Two department heads with equal authority disagree over how to share a fixed training budget. A decision is needed by tomorrow, and each agrees to give up part of their request. Which mode is this?
C.why: Each side giving up part of what it wanted, to reach a quick, workable answer between equals, is compromising.

whyNot.0: Collaborating would look for a solution fully satisfying both, which needs more time.
whyNot.2: Neither simply gives way to the other.
whyNot.3: Neither imposes their view on the other.

C.q: A crucial architecture decision will shape the system for ten years. Two expert teams disagree, both have valuable insights, and there are three weeks before it must be made. Which mode suits best?
C.why: An important issue, time available, and expertise on both sides all point to collaborating, for a solution both teams are committed to.

whyNot.0: Imposing one view throws away the other team's insights.
whyNot.1: Avoiding a crucial decision only delays and worsens the problem.
whyNot.3: Simply giving way loses one team's valuable insight.

C.q: Which statement about the Thomas-Kilmann modes is NOT correct?
C.why: No mode is always best. Collaborating takes time and effort, so it is wasted on trivial issues and too slow for emergencies.

whyNot.0: This is correct: avoiding suits trivial issues or cooling off.
whyNot.1: This is correct: competing suits emergencies and quick decisions.
whyNot.3: This is correct: the skill is choosing the mode that fits.

reteach.title: Five flatmates and one TV
reteach.question: Five flatmates all want the TV on Saturday night. How might each one handle it, and when would each approach be sensible?

blocks.body: Sam grabs the remote: the cup final is on and it's now or never (competing). Priya suggests streaming the film in the kitchen so both groups get what they want (collaborating). Tom offers: first half football, then the film (compromising). Lou shrugs and goes out: it's only telly (avoiding). Ben lets Sam have it because he picked last week and wants to stay friends (accommodating). Each is sensible in the right moment.

blocks.text: Lou (avoiding) and Ben (accommodating) both end up without the TV, but for different reasons: Lou doesn't engage at all; Ben actively helps Sam get what he wants.

explain.body: Assertiveness: how far you try to satisfy your own concerns. Cooperativeness: how far you try to satisfy the other party's concerns. Every mode is a mix of the two.

rows.label: High means
values: Helping them get what they want

test.q: In the Thomas-Kilmann model, what does cooperativeness measure?
options: Effort to meet your own concerns
test.why: Cooperativeness is the extent to which you try to satisfy the other party's concerns.

whyNot.1: Satisfying your own concerns is assertiveness.
whyNot.2: Escalation is not one of the TKI dimensions.
whyNot.3: Speed is not a TKI dimension; it is a factor in choosing a mode.

explain.body: Competing (high assertive, low cooperative) pushes your own position: right for emergencies and quick, unpopular decisions. Avoiding (low on both) sidesteps or postpones: right for trivial issues or when people need to cool off, but issues can fester.

test.q: What is the main risk of a project manager relying too heavily on avoiding?
options: Solutions take too long to agree
test.why: Avoiding sidesteps conflict, so if overused, important issues are left to grow and fester.

whyNot.0: Avoiding usually means fewer, not more, meetings about the issue.
whyNot.2: Feeling overruled is the risk of competing.
whyNot.3: Slow agreement is the risk of collaborating.

explain.body: Accommodating (low assertive, high cooperative) gives way to the other party: right when you are wrong or the relationship matters more. Compromising (moderate on both) splits the difference: right for expedient or temporary fixes, especially between equals under time pressure.

test.q: Which mode is described as 'splitting the difference'?
test.why: Compromising finds a middle ground where each side gives up part of what it wanted.

whyNot.0: Collaborating seeks a solution that fully satisfies both sides.
whyNot.1: Accommodating gives the other party what they want.
whyNot.3: Avoiding doesn't engage with the conflict at all.

explain.body: Collaborating (high on both) works through the issue to find a win-win: right for important issues when time allows and commitment matters. The wider lesson: diagnose importance, relationship, time and power, then choose the mode to suit the situation.

test.q: According to the Thomas-Kilmann approach, how should a project manager decide which conflict mode to use?
options: Let the most senior person decide
Match the mode to the situation
test.why: Each mode suits different circumstances, so the project manager diagnoses the situation and selects the mode that fits.

whyNot.0: A default mode will often be the wrong tool.
whyNot.1: Collaborating is too slow for emergencies and wasteful for trivial issues.
whyNot.2: Seniority alone doesn't determine the best way to handle a conflict.
